text: Every lesson in this chapter builds toward one famous result, so it starts with the problem itself: given a composite number N, find its prime factors. That sentence sounds almost too simple to matter — but the difficulty of answering it classically is the entire reason RSA encryption has protected internet traffic for decades.

Given a composite N, find p and q such that N equals p times q. Multiplying two large primes together is computationally cheap; reversing that multiplication is, as far as anyone has proven classically, dramatically harder. That asymmetry is called a one-way function, and it's exactly what RSA exploits: the public key includes N, the private key depends on p and q individually, and an attacker who could factor N back into its primes could reconstruct the private key and break the encryption entirely. This is a claim about computational difficulty, not mathematical impossibility.

The best known classical algorithm, the General Number Field Sieve, runs in time roughly exponential of n to the one-third times log n to the two-thirds for an n-bit number — sub-exponential, meaningfully faster than brute force, but still not polynomial. That's exactly why doubling RSA's key size, from 1024 to 2048 bits, made factoring dramatically harder in practice, not just twice as hard. Shor's algorithm, by contrast, factors in roughly O of n cubed gate operations — polynomial time.

Recall Grover's algorithm from Chapter 4: a quadratic speedup where classical and quantum running times stay in the same complexity class, just with different exponents. Shor's algorithm is categorically different — it moves factoring from sub-exponential into polynomial outright, changing which problems are tractable at all as N grows. That's the reason factoring specifically is the result that made cryptographers pay attention to quantum computing.

Next lesson shows exactly how: Shor's algorithm doesn't factor N directly, it solves a completely different-looking problem, finding a hidden period, and shows that solving that one solves factoring almost for free.
